# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–2 (Complete and Final – Updated 51)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; now nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; now summer of first year
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring
- **Atmospheric Details**: Bell for vespers ringing thinly; road rutted and puddled after thaw; wind off water with salt and tar smell; frost silvering hedges; chalk sun on forge wall; smoke from chimneys lying flat; turnip carts passing; dog barking periodically; river up in spring

## Main Characters

**Dorothea**
- Recently widowed; residing at Lowick Manor
- **Financial Status**: Seven hundred a-year personal fortune; nineteen hundred a-year from Casaubon; three to four thousand ready money in bank; dislikes Casaubon's property
- **Conviction About Lydgate**: Feels convinced Lydgate's conduct not guilty
- **Plan to Help Lydgate**: Wrote brief note with check for thousand pounds
- **Discovery at Lydgate's House**: Saw Will seated with Rosamond close by, flushed and tearful, Will clasping her hands with low-toned fervor; laid down letter and left quickly
- **Night of Anguish**: Waves of suffering shaking her thoroughly; cried in loud whispers between sobs; lay on bare floor as night grew cold; saw two images—Rosamond and Will—tearing her heart
- **Morning Awakening**: Awoke with clearest consciousness of looking into eyes of sorrow; wrapped warm things around her; seated in great chair; soul liberated from terrible conflict; could sit with grief as lasting companion
- **Second Visit to Lydgate's House**: Spoke about injustice shown Lydgate; spoke quite simply, gathering firmness; experienced emotional breaking point; clasped Rosamond as if in shipwreck; experienced revulsion of feeling too strong to be called joy; immediate consciousness one of immense sympathy without check
- **Revelation from Rosamond**: Rosamond disclosed Will loves another woman (Dorothea); said Will claims no other woman existed beside Dorothea; said blame entirely hers; said he cannot reproach her anymore
- **Evening Encounter with Will in Library**: Could not receive him where husband's prohibition seemed to dwell; when door opened, did not move; he came towards her with doubt and timidity; Dorothea afraid of her own emotion; stood motionless, hindering her from unclasping her hands
- **Will's Explanation**: Affair now matter of gossip; idea of getting Bulstrode to apply money to public purpose brought him back; Bulstrode privately offered compensation for old injury and good income; told her if it were new hardship, new reason to cling to her; nothing could have changed him but thinking she was different, not so good as believed; said she would believe him better than he is except in one thing—his truth to her
- **Storm Scene and Hand-Clasping**: Stood silent with Will looking at evergreens tossed showing pale underside against blackening sky; lightning made them start and smile; when vivid flash lit each for other, Dorothea darted instantaneously from window; Will seized her hand with spasmodic movement; they stood with hands clasped like two children; turned faces towards each other with memory of his last words in them
- **Will's Despairing Words**: Said there is no hope for him; even if she loved him as well as he loves her, he shall most likely always be very poor; on sober calculation, creeping lot only certain; impossible they ever belong to each other; perhaps base of him to have asked for word; meant to go away into silence but has not been able
- **Will's Continued Bitterness**: Said it is cruel of her to speak that way; she may see beyond misery but he doesn't; it is unkind—throwing back his love as if trifle; they can never be married; mere toss up whether he shall ever do more than keep himself decently unless sells himself as pen and mouthpiece; could not offer himself to any woman, even if she had no luxuries to renounce
- **Heart Full of Words**: Her heart full of something she wanted to say but words too difficult; wholly possessed by them; debate was mute within her; very hard she could not say what she wanted
- **Will's Departure and Her Response**: Will looked out of window angrily; at last turned and stretched hand automatically towards hat, said with exasperation "Good-by"; in instant she spoke; Will had arms round her but she drew head back and held his away gently while speaking; large tear-filled eyes looking at his very simply; spoke in sobbing childlike way: "We could live quite well on my own fortune—it is too much—seven hundred a-year—I want so little—no new clothes—and I will learn what everything costs"
- **Engagement and Plans**: Sent for uncle Mr. Brooke to Lowick; matter came about quite suddenly—neither had any idea two days ago; quite determined to act as she likes; Mr. Brooke will give her away but plans to cut off entail (will cost money and be troublesome)
- **Celia's Visit to Lowick**: Celia traveled to Lowick to influence Dorothea's mind; through girlhood felt she could act on her by word judiciously placed; as matron felt more able to advise childless sister; expressed shock at decision; said she has disappointed them all; said very bad; questioned how can marry Ladislaw with no estate; noted it shocks James dreadfully; called it all so different from what Dorothea has always been; referenced former reasons for marrying Casaubon (great soul, learning, age, dismalness) and expressed bewilderment at marrying Ladislaw instead

**Will Ladislaw**
- Passionate love for Dorothea
- **Public Scandal**: Genealogy now public knowledge via Bambridge's disclosure; described as having "queer genealogy"—high-spirited young lady, musical Polish patriot, with "grafting of the Jew pawnbroker"
- **Scene at Lydgate's House**: Seated with Rosamond on sofa, clasping both her upraised hands, speaking with low-toned fervor; when Rosamond became aware of Dorothea and snatched away her hands, Will looked round; meeting Dorothea's eyes with new lightning in them, seemed changing to marble
- **Anguish After Dorothea's Departure**: Stood motionless with Rosamond; looked towards spot where Dorothea stood; said sharply "Don't touch me!" with utterance like cut of lash; darted from Rosamond; wheeled round to other side of room with tips of fingers in pockets and head thrown back, looking fiercely; expressed inability to explain passion and that no other woman existed beside Dorothea
- **Plans to Return to Middlemarch**: As exile, had placed no stronger obstacle to return than own resolve—not iron barrier but state of mind liable to melt; as months went on, seemed more difficult to say why should not run down merely to hear something about Dorothea; hunger had tamed him and became very hungry for vision of certain form and sound of certain voice; took Riverston coach and came back again; made up mind he must go to Lydgate's that evening
- **Visit to Lydgate's House**: Received by Rosamond with languid coldness; Rosamond sat in silence bending over work; when poured tea, placed tiny bit of folded paper in his saucer; he secured it quickly; opened and read it by bed-candle; effect made cheeks and ears burn thinking of what occurred between Dorothea and Rosamond; felt uncertainty how far Dorothea might still feel dignity wounded; feared lasting flaw in her mind
- **Evening in Library with Dorothea**: Came towards her with more doubt and timidity than she had ever seen, afraid lest some look or word condemn him to new distance; took her hand and raised it to his lips with something like a sob; stood with hat and gloves in other hand; difficult to loose hand; felt very happy leaning on chair, not much afraid of anything she might feel; stood silent not looking at each other but at evergreens tossed showing pale underside of leaves; lightning made them start and smile; when vivid flash lit each for other, seized her hand with spasmodic movement; they stood with hands clasped like two children; turned faces towards each other; did not loose each other's hands
- **Expressions of Despair**: Said must be that they can never be married; it is cruel of her to speak that way—as if there were any comfort; it is unkind—throwing back his love as if trifle; expressed mere toss up whether shall ever do more than keep himself decently unless sells himself as pen and mouthpiece; could not offer himself to any woman, even if she had no luxuries to renounce; looked out of window angrily; at last turned, still resting against chair, and stretching hand automatically towards hat, said with exasperation, "Good-by"
- **Reversal When Dorothea Speaks**: When she spoke in sobbing childlike way about living well on her own fortune of seven hundred a-year, wanting so little, no new clothes, willing to learn what everything costs, Will had arms round her
- **Engagement**: Now engaged to marry Dorothea; has "objectionable position" and "bad origin" per Sir James

**Lydgate**
- **Moral Crisis**: Constructed probabilities case—Bulstrode feared scandalous disclosures from Raffles; may have tampered with patient or disobeyed orders; acknowledges "just possible" sometimes true; questions whether would have acted identically without money
- **Social Ostracism**: Patients avoiding him; practice and reputation utterly damned; general black-balling begun
- **Interview with Dorothea**: Told her everything from first application to Bulstrode under pressure of difficulties; disclosed his doubts and uneasy consciousness that accepting money made some difference in private inclination; wrote letter of gratitude
- **Final Resolution**: Declines continuing at Hospital; must get away from Middlemarch as soon as possible
- **Evening with Will**: Will arrived looking rather battered; felt inexpressibly mournful discussing settling in London
- **Return Home and Rosamond's Illness**: Found Rosamond ill on bed, soothed and tended her for next hour
- **Morning After**: Saw Dorothea's letter on drawing-room table with check for thousand pounds; Rosamond made no reply when he mentioned Ladislaw sat with him last night
- **Second Visit from Dorothea**: Led her to drawing-room, put his letter of gratitude into her hands, then went upstairs; told Rosamond gently Mrs. Casaubon had come to see her again; when returned after going to Coleman's, noticed both women needed care; offered to order Dorothea's carriage
- **Evening Scene**: Has accepted his narrowed lot with sad resignation; chosen fragile Rosamond and taken burden of her life upon his arms; must walk carrying that burden pitifully; felt thankful when Rosamond showed little mark of interest in him, pushing back his hair; prepared Rosamond's room for evening; when Will visited evening and Rosamond poured tea, Lydgate innocently remained in room and noticed nothing amiss; apologized indirectly for Rosamond's exhaustion by suggesting she rest; is full of timid care for his wife, not only because he deprecated any harshness of judgment from her, but because he felt deep distress at sight of her suffering

**Rosamond Lydgate**
- Married to Lydgate; victorious obstinacy never wasting energy
- **Crisis Response**: When scandal broke, shock was terrible; felt shame was worst part of crime; regained brilliant health; determined to tell Will Ladislaw everything when he comes; morning descended equipped for walk with letter to Mr. Ladislaw written with charming discretion
- **Scene with Will**: With bonnet hanging back, sat flushed and tearful, turned towards Will who leaned towards her clasping both her upraised hands; when Dorothea entered, snatched away her hands and rose; under first great shock that shattered her dream-world; strange unexpected manifestation of Dorothea's feeling made her soul totter
- **Will's Anger**: Had no sense of chill resolute repulsion such as known under Lydgate's displeasure; all her sensibility turned into bewildering novelty of pain; felt new terrified recoil under lash never experienced before; became image of sickened misery with pale lips and eyes with tearless dismay
- **Morning After**: Sat languidly wondering what to do next; looked ill but recovered her usual quietude; made no reply when Lydgate told her of Dorothea's letter with check and that Ladislaw sat with him
- **Response to Dorothea's Second Visit**: Colored and gave startled movement when Lydgate said Mrs. Casaubon come to see her again; did not say no despite daring not touch yesterday's facts; Will's lacerating words made every thought of Dorothea fresh smart; in humiliating uncertainty dared do nothing but comply; pride broken down between the two women; disclosed to Dorothea that Will loves another woman (Dorothea), told her she has told Dorothea and he cannot reproach her anymore; asked "Tertius did not find fault with me, then?" understanding Lydgate might have said anything to Mrs. Casaubon; smile began to play over Dorothea's face; poor Rosamond's vagrant fancy come back terribly scourged—meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; shelter was still there; her husband had accepted his narrowed lot with sad resignation
- **This Evening**: Prepared for Will's visit; received him with languid coldness; sat in silence bending over bit of work; when poured tea and Will came near, placed tiny bit of folded paper in his saucer; had written note to him with neatly flowing hand
- **Context**: Has sent her daughters away to board at school on coast that this crisis might be hidden from them as far as possible; set free by their absence from intolerable necessity of accounting for her grief or beholding their frightened wonder; she could live unconstrainedly with sorrow that was every day streaking her hair with whiteness and making her eyelids languid

## Family Reactions to Engagement

**Sir James Chettam**: Still in white indignation; said if Ladislaw had spark of honor would have gone out of country at once; said not surprised, day after Casaubon's funeral said what ought to be done but not listened to; unable to repress retort; called it perfectly scandalous, saying Dorothea degrading herself by marrying him; emphasized delicacy ought to have forbidden her seeing him again after husband's will; listed grievances: Ladislaw takes her from proper rank into poverty, has meanness to accept such sacrifice, always had objectionable position, bad origin, man of little principle and light character; said cannot take Ladislaw into family and must speak for himself; acknowledged to himself (though ashamed) part of opposition stems from jealous repugnance not entirely different from his reaction to Casaubon; acknowledges marriage fatal for Dorothea; also motivated by undeniable fact that union of two estates—Tipton and Freshitt—lying charmingly within ring-fence was prospect that flattered him for his son and heir; when Mr. Brooke mentioned cutting off entail, Sir James felt sudden embarrassment, stoppage in throat, blushed; found more words than usual in first jet of anger, but Mr. Brooke's propitiation more clogging to his tongue than Mrs. Cadwallader's caustic hint

**Mr. Brooke** (Dorothea's uncle): Tried to dissuade her, pointed out poverty and abandoning position, said "My dear, you don't know what it is to live on seven hundred a-year, and have no carriage, and that kind of thing, and go amongst people who don't know who you are"; spoke strongly to her but she quite determined to act as she likes; looking dejected at Freshitt Hall, came forward with evident nervous perturbation; told family about Dorothea—went to Lowick after she sent for him; it had come about quite suddenly—neither had any idea two days ago; he put it strongly to her, did his duty, but she can act as she likes; advised Sir James to talk to Dorothea herself; mentioned fact that she has dislike to Casaubon's property; can cut off the entail; will cost money and be troublesome; he showed his own force of resolution and propitiated what was just in Baronet's vexation; touched a motive of which Sir James was ashamed

**Mr. Cadwallader** (Rector): Said to be just to Chettam; objected to all unnecessary discomfort; acknowledged Mrs. Casaubon may be acting imprudently, giving up fortune for man, but said should not condemn as wrong action in strict sense because men have such poor opinion of each other; said they are rather apt to consider act wrong because it is unpleasant to them; like many men who take life easily, had knack of saying home truth occasionally to those who felt themselves virtuously out of temper; said should not make any fuss about it, if she likes to be poor that is her affair; said nobody would have said anything if she had married young fellow because he was rich; noted plenty of beneficed clergy are poorer than they will be; referenced his own case: had hardly thousand a-year, was lout, nobody could see anything in him, shoes were not right cut, all men wondered how woman could like him; said must take Ladislaw's part until hearing more harm of him

**Mrs. Cadwallader**: Noted "there is usually a silent exception in such cases"; said only wonder to her is that any of them are surprised; blamed them for doing nothing to hinder it; said if they had had Lord Triton down here to woo her with his philanthropy, he might have carried her off before year was over; said "There was no safety in anything else"; blamed Mr. Casaubon for preparing it all beautifully by making himself disagreeable or it pleasing God to make him so, then daring her to contradict him; said it is way to make any trumpery tempting, to ticket it at high price in that way

**Celia Chettam**: Thought it would be of great use to take journey to Lowick to influence Dorothea's mind; through girlhood felt she could act on her sister by word judiciously placed; as matron naturally felt more able to advise her childless sister; said to Dorothea it is very bad, you have disappointed us all so; expressed disbelief that marriage "ever will be"—Dorothea never can go live in that way; referenced all her plans; noted James would have taken any trouble for her and she might have gone on all her life doing what she liked; noted Dorothea always wanted things that wouldn't do, but other plans would have come; expressed shock: "how can you marry Mr. Ladislaw, that we none of us ever thought you could marry? It shocks James so dreadfully. And then it is all so different from what you have always been. You would have Mr. Casaubon because he had such a great soul, and was so old and dismal and learned; and now, to think of marrying Mr. Ladislaw, who has got no estate or anything. I suppose it is because you must be making yourself uncomfortable in some way or other."

## Bulstrode Family Matters

**Mr. Bulstrode**: Has told his wife (Harriet) he intends not to sell the land he possesses in this neighborhood, but to leave it to her as safe provision; discussed with her possibility of making amends to Rosamond and her husband; Lydgate must leave town, his practice is almost good for nothing, they have very little left to settle anywhere with; mentioned Garth once thought of undertaking management of Stone Court in order to place nephew Fred there; stock to remain as is, they to pay certain share of profits instead of ordinary rent; suggested this desirable beginning for young man in conjunction with employment under Garth; told Harriet she must make proposal to Garth herself, that land is virtually hers and Garth need have no transactions with him; communications can be made through Standish; mentioned Garth gave up being his agent; can put into her hands paper which Garth himself drew up, stating conditions; she can propose his renewed acceptance of them; thinks not unlikely Garth will accept when she proposes it for sake of nephew

**Harriet Bulstrode** (Mrs. Bulstrode): Expressed wish to do something for her brother's family (Fred and Mary Garth); thinks they are bound to make some amends to Rosamond and her husband; said she would rather do without something for themselves to make some amends to her poor brother's family; mentioned Walter (presumably her brother) says Mr. Lydgate must leave town; the letter (Mrs. Casaubon's check) seemed to cut her severely; the mention of Mrs. Casaubon's loan seemed a reflection of public feeling which held it matter of course that everyone would avoid connection with her husband; she was silent for some time; tears fell one after the other, her chin trembling as she wiped them away; Bulstrode, sitting opposite, ached at sight of that grief-worn face, which two months before had been bright and blooming; it had aged to keep sad company with his own withered features

## Garth Family Matters

**Mary Garth**: Has been single and merry for four-and-twenty years and more; supposed it will not be quite as long again as that; mind quite settled regarding marriage; said "Not a sad while, father—I mean to be merry"; expressed willingness: "If you are contented with Fred?"; bent her face before father's more gravely; Caleb returned to his first tone asking if there's no other wish come into her mind since things have been going on as they have of late (Caleb meant a great deal in that vague phrase); Caleb said "because, better late than never. A woman must not force her heart—she'll do a man no good by that."

**Caleb Garth**: Has tender concern for Mary's contentment; wants to ensure her mind is quite settled; inquires whether any other wish has come into it since things have been going on as they have been of late; expresses belief that a woman must not force her heart—she'll do a man no good by that

**Fred Garth**: Is involved in employment under Caleb; referenced as nephew who might benefit from management of Stone Court arrangement proposed by Bulstrode through Harriet

## Rumors and Unverified Claims
- Wife of Ridan Corrett confided late one night to Ilzek Wexwood that the bridge toll at Salwick is skimmed every month [NOTE: This matches earlier rumor attributed to Breena Orlwood]
- Gossip from Pebin Wexwood claimed Thidrek Corrett and Rira Stenworth had been wed in secret
- Earlier rumors preserved: Lindson blood debt to Hollmere; Lindson mill ledger rewritten after flood; Salford granary fire set on purpose; old abbey at Salford second cellar; Bryngate pastures deed forged; silver chest buried beneath Mirecombe well; Quenwick chapel vault opens only for living person with jade ring and oak comb; Dunholt toll bridge belonged to Wexwood family

## Minor Characters and Incidental Details
- Eldette Corrett, Ridan Corrett, Breena Orlwood, Breena (unknown surname), Daena Wexwood, Jotho Corrett, Pebin Wexwood, Cobin, Nyrine (no surname given), Pebin Wexwood (appears twice): Various townspeople mentioned briefly in atmospheric fragments; Daena Wexwood argued with carter over price of sack of oats; Pebin Wexwood watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly; Eldette walked long way round to avoid muddy square; Breena Orlwood complained of aching back; Pebin mended torn sleeve by window and said little; Pebin counted coins twice and still came up a penny short; The price of salt is a scandal according to Eldette, agreed by Cobin; Will it rain, do you think? asked Breena; Nyrine read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints; Pebin noted river was up again per Daena Wexwood; Jotho Corrett said it always was in spring
